# AURORA Agent — full corpus for LLM consumption

Canonical site: https://aurora-neuro.github.io/aurora-agent/
Repository: https://github.com/AURORA-NEURO/aurora-agent (public, Apache-2.0)
Engine crates are prefixed `bioprism-`; binaries are `bioprism`, `bioprism-mcp`, `bioprism-api`.

Research and developer infrastructure: it does not diagnose an individual, recommend treatment,
triage care, enroll participants, or claim medical-device functionality.

---

## What it is

AURORA Agent is a Rust workspace of 79 crates implementing the FIBER decision-context compiler.
The central idea, from README.md: context assembly is a compiler pass — instead of retrieval plus
summarisation plus vibes-based compaction, a typed decision query is compiled into the smallest
decision-sufficient evidence region, delivered as a Decision Section, and accompanied by a Context
Certificate that states exactly what was omitted and whether the omission could have changed the
decision.

The README's motto: "Compile the smallest decision-sufficient evidence region. Never traverse the
whole knowledge structure by default."

Surfaces:

- 259 MCP tools via the `bioprism-mcp` stdio server (JSON-RPC 2.0 over newline-delimited stdio,
  full MCP lifecycle).
- A CLI (`bioprism`), with `--json` envelopes and a 10-exit-code retryability matrix: every failure
  code carries exactly one retry decision, so a caller holding nothing but the process status can
  decide whether to re-send.
- A local HTTP gateway (`bioprism-api`) for deployments that need a network boundary.

Privacy: fully local. No network access, no external services, no telemetry, no data collection.
Policy: https://github.com/AURORA-NEURO/aurora-agent/blob/main/PRIVACY.md

---

## The headline benchmark is a deliberate negative

This is the product thesis, stated plainly and never spun.

Reference-world measurement (from README.md and docs/FINDINGS.md): the reference world ships 761
facts, 750 of them exploratory distractors that all consume the same protected `cohort_id` hub.
FIBER compiles the query down to 11 facts — 1.45% of the world — and the deterministic oracle
still returns the correct verdict with all four leakage witnesses.

It is not alone in doing so. Under equal tuning, a 5-hop incidence walk and a BM25 retriever at
k=11 select exactly the same eleven facts — not the same count, the identical set. On the shipped
reference world, FIBER has no measurable advantage over a correctly tuned graph walk or a lexical
retriever. docs/FINDINGS.md notes that the distribution's own `compare_baselines.py` measured the
graph baseline only at depth 7 and unbounded — the two settings where it returns everything — and
reported a 69x advantage that vanishes under equal tuning; the workspace corrects that strawman.

FIBER only wins on the generated discriminating world. `crates/worldgen` makes world structure a
parameter and builds a world that can tell the methods apart: distractors attached near the target
instead of at a hub leaf, decisive facts behind a relay chain, and distractor tags camouflaged to
tokenise into the protected vocabulary. On that world (docs/DISCRIMINATING_COMPARISON.md, summarised
in docs/FINDINGS.md):

| Strategy               | Facts | Sound? | Closure | Admissible |
|------------------------|------:|:------:|--------:|:----------:|
| full-context           |   762 |  yes   |    100% |    yes     |
| graph-5-hop            |   750 |  no    |      0% |    no      |
| graph-7-hop            |   750 |  no    |      0% |    no      |
| lexical-top-11 (BM25)  |    11 |  yes   |     91% |    no      |
| fiber                  |    11 |  yes   |    100% |    yes     |

Three distinct failure modes appear. The graph walk has no usable depth: depths 5-10 pull in 98%
of the world and still miss every decisive witness. BM25 reaches the right verdict from a 91%
protected closure — right by luck, having dropped a protected fact that happened not to matter, and
raising k to 50 never recovers it. FIBER is the cheapest admissible strategy — right verdict and
full closure at 11 facts. That last failure mode is why the harness ranks on admissibility rather than
verdict alone — ranking on verdict would have crowned the strategy that violated the mandatory
closure and got away with it.

docs/FINDINGS.md is explicit about the limits: this does not establish that FIBER wins generally.
The discriminating world was built to expose exactly these failure modes, just as the reference
world was built to expose hub expansion. Both are single points; the full structural sweep is not
done, and an embedding retriever and a directed dependency walk are still missing from the panel.

---

## Cross-language parity

Certificate hashes are taken over canonical bytes, so implementations must agree exactly or a
certificate produced by one cannot be replayed by another. The reference parity digest

    c0da17ffc80465258345c8a538171bfd868100cd883e9a20780a0dc5477e7ea4

is agreed by three implementations: the CPython reference runtime, the Rust eager path, and the
Rust indexed store. Per README.md, getting there required matching CPython in two places a naive
port gets wrong: `repr` float formatting (CPython switches to exponential at a different threshold
than Rust and zero-pads the exponent) and JSON object iteration order, which the reference relies
on when building leakage witnesses.

---

## Installing

- MCP registry: listed as `io.github.MurariAmbati/aurora-agent` v0.1.1 on
  registry.modelcontextprotocol.io.
- Claude Desktop: download `aurora-agent.mcpb` (v0.1.1, Windows-only prebuilt) from
  https://github.com/AURORA-NEURO/aurora-agent/releases and double-click it (or Settings ->
  Extensions). sha256 e987c396a01eb2ae812efa8226f6892fc3f70cb441102217476990816458f025. It ships
  with the reference fixtures; the "AURORA data root" setting can point at a full checkout.
- Claude Code: the repository is a plugin marketplace —
  `claude plugin marketplace add AURORA-NEURO/aurora-agent` then
  `claude plugin install aurora-agent@aurora`.
- From source: `cargo build --release --offline`, then run `./target/release/bioprism-mcp --root .`
  for the MCP server or use the `bioprism` CLI directly.

## Quickstart (CLI, from README.md)

    cargo build --release --offline
    ./target/release/bioprism context explain \
      --world fixtures/fiber-v0.1/radiogenomic_world.json \
      --query fixtures/fiber-v0.1/leakage_query.json

That prints a database-style explain plan: which passes ran and what each retained, the backend,
selection ratios, omissions grouped by influence class, the oracle verdict with its witnesses, and
which passes did not run and why.

    ./target/release/bioprism --json context compile \
      --world fixtures/fiber-v0.1/radiogenomic_world.json \
      --query fixtures/fiber-v0.1/leakage_query.json --certificate-out cert.json
    ./target/release/bioprism context verify --certificate cert.json

Scale: compiling from a JSON document parses the whole world on every query. `bioprism world
index --world big-world.json --store big-world.bpw` indexes it once; `--world` then accepts the
store directory anywhere it accepted a document, and the certificate is identical. Per README.md,
on a one-million-fact world this takes query time from 26.5 s to 41.6 ms, and compile cost becomes
roughly logarithmic in corpus size rather than linear (reasoning in docs/ADR-001-language-strategy.md).

## Exit codes (README.md)

Ten codes; every failure code carries exactly one retry decision. `bioprism --help` prints the
table; `--json` puts the same decision in the envelope as `error.retryability`.

| code | name             | retry decision         |
|-----:|------------------|------------------------|
|    0 | ok               | — (verdict, not failure) |
|    1 | assertion_failed | — (verdict, not failure) |
|    2 | usage            | terminal               |
|    3 | invalid_input    | terminal               |
|    4 | compile_failed   | retryable_after_change |
|    5 | io               | retryable_as_is        |
|    6 | conflict         | terminal               |
|    7 | policy_denied    | retryable_after_change |
|    8 | indeterminate    | retryable_after_change |
|    9 | stale            | retryable_as_is        |

---

## Using it from an agent (README.md)

`bioprism-mcp --root .` speaks JSON-RPC 2.0 over newline-delimited stdio and follows the MCP
lifecycle. `fiber_compile` returns the L0 decision contract — goal, verdict, what was omitted,
whether the sufficiency claim holds — plus a versioned, content-addressed refinement handle, and
not the evidence. An agent passes that handle to `fiber_refine` only when the contract is
insufficient to act; the server recompiles and verifies the certificate digest before disclosing
the requested layer. On the reference world L0 is ~204 estimated tokens against ~1,900 for the
full section.

The invariant that makes that safe: omissions are reported at every layer, so an agent that stops
at L0 still knows what it does not have. Layering hides volume, never the fact of an omission.
Paths are confined to `--root`; absolute paths, `..`, and symlink escapes are refused. Shipped
JSON schemas and the capability catalog are available through read-only MCP resources.

Beyond FIBER compilation, the tool surface spans world validation and generation, equal-engineering
baseline comparison (`context_compare`), metamorphic mutation families, benchmark-pack registry and
release gates, evaluation and oracle combination, oncology-domain boundary checks, policy and
safety screening, epistemic value-of-information planning, capability discovery/routing/dashboard,
and mission preflight and execution with digest-bound plans. Domain tools consistently preserve
refusals, omissions, and non-claims rather than collapsing them into scores; a completed local
call is never promoted into a readiness, scientific, or clinical verdict.

The repository also ships a dependency-free Python client (`python/`, docs/PYTHON_SDK.md) with
synchronous and asyncio MCP sessions plus an HTTP client, and a dependency-free TypeScript Fetch
client (`typescript/`, docs/TYPESCRIPT_SDK.md) for browser and Node consumers.

## HTTP gateway (docs/HTTP_API.md)

`bioprism-api` is the network-facing integration layer over the Rust MCP server, available as a
library and a binary:

    cargo run -p bioprism-api -- --root . --bind 127.0.0.1:8787 --token <at-least-16-visible-bytes>

The gateway is intentionally bounded and one-request-per-connection: headers default to 32 KiB,
bodies to 2 MiB, event retention to 4,096 entries, and every route reports an `X-Request-Id`.
Bearer authentication protects every route except `/healthz`, `/readyz`, and the OpenAPI document.
It exposes the exact MCP tool catalogue through REST and JSON-RPC, capability routing and
dashboard routes, bounded mission jobs with typed status polling and cooperative cancellation,
cursor-addressable event pages/SSE snapshots, and signed webhook outbox lifecycle. It deliberately
reports gRPC, TLS termination, distributed scheduling, and external delivery as absent rather than
inferring them from an HTTP listener.

---

## Architecture (docs/ARCHITECTURE.md)

Layers, top to bottom: agent surface (cli, mcp) -> evaluation (prism, baseline, mutation,
registry) -> composition (weave) -> compilation (fiber, section) -> world and storage (world,
store, worldgen, adapter, bioir, onco, oracle) -> foundation (ids, scope).

Why the boundaries fall where they do:

- `ids` depends on nothing. Certificates hash canonical bytes and cross-language byte parity is
  hard, so there is one canonical implementation at the root of the graph.
- `section` depends on neither `world` nor `fiber`. A consumer — an MCP client, a CI gate, an
  auditor — must be able to read and verify a compiled context without linking the engine that
  produced it.
- `fiber` is generic over `WorldSource`: the same query compiled against an in-memory world and
  against an indexed store must produce byte-identical certificates, asserted in
  `crates/store/tests/store_parity.rs`.
- `weave`'s kernel is small on purpose: a trusted computing base that enforces identity, protocol
  legality, authority, budgets and causal ordering, and explicitly does not decide what is true.
- `baseline` exists to make the central claim falsifiable. Without competent comparators, "FIBER
  compiles a smaller context" is unfalsifiable. With them it came out a draw on the reference world.

Cross-crate invariants each pinned by a test include: canonical bytes match CPython exactly;
eager and indexed backends agree byte for byte; protected closure is computed before any relevance
step; zero influence is distinguishable from unknown influence; a budget smaller than the closure
fails rather than truncating; omissions are reported at every disclosure layer; a nondeterministic
judgement cannot overturn a deterministic one; a mutation cannot validate its own postcondition;
an adapter must declare what it could not preserve; a pack cannot be promoted past its evidence.

What is not there: no network layer in the kernel, no multi-tenancy, no hosted execution —
local-first only. Heavy biological formats (DICOM, BIDS/NIfTI, AnnData/Zarr, VCF) belong in a
Python layer per ADR-001; the Rust side owns the adapter contract, not the parsers.

## Capability dashboard (docs/CAPABILITY_DASHBOARD.md)

`capability_dashboard` is the operator-facing projection between the workspace catalogue,
authoritative MCP schemas, and the SDK/CLI surface declarations. It answers a practical question
before an agent builds a mission: which domains are actually callable through this transport,
which are only declared, and what surface is missing. Every group row is classified independently
as `callable`, `partial`, or `declared_only`, with separate counts for crates, MCP memberships,
CLI entrypoints, and Python artifacts. Gaps are labels, not a blended quality score.
`capability_dashboard_ready` does not grant permission, prove scientific validity, execute a tool,
or establish deployment readiness. Non-executing HTTP planning endpoints
(`/v1/capabilities/route`, `/route/review`, `/route/plan`, `/route/plan/verify`) compose route
review with authoritative mission preflight; `dispatch` remains `not_started`.

---

## FAQ

Q: What problem does AURORA Agent solve?
A: Deciding what context an agent actually needs. Instead of retrieving and summarising, FIBER
compiles a typed decision query into the smallest decision-sufficient evidence region and issues a
Context Certificate stating exactly what was omitted and whether the omission could have changed
the decision.

Q: Is FIBER better than retrieval baselines?
A: On the shipped reference world, no — that is the headline result, reported deliberately. A
5-hop graph walk, BM25 at k=11, and FIBER select the identical eleven facts there. FIBER separates
from both only on the generated discriminating world, where it is the cheapest admissible strategy
(right verdict and 100% protected closure at 11 facts). Neither single world establishes a general
win; the full structural sweep is not done.

Q: What does "admissible" mean in the benchmarks?
A: Sound (the strategy's selection, fed to the same deterministic oracle, reproduces the
full-context verdict with the same leakage witnesses) and complete closure (all of the query's
protected facts retained). The harness ranks on admissibility rather than verdict alone, because
a strategy can reach the right verdict from an incomplete protected basis by luck.

Q: How do I install it?
A: Claude Desktop: the `aurora-agent.mcpb` (Windows-only prebuilt) from the GitHub releases page.
Claude Code: `claude plugin marketplace add AURORA-NEURO/aurora-agent` then
`claude plugin install aurora-agent@aurora`. MCP registry: `io.github.MurariAmbati/aurora-agent`
v0.1.1. From source: `cargo build --release --offline`.

Q: Does it phone home?
A: No. It is a local program: no network requests, no external services, no telemetry, no
analytics, no crash reporting, no account. The optional `bioprism-api` gateway binds to an address
you choose (loopback by default) and serves only callers presenting your bearer token.

Q: Can I use it for clinical decisions?
A: No. Research and developer infrastructure: it does not diagnose an individual, recommend
treatment, triage care, enroll participants, or claim medical-device functionality. The
`medical_boundary_check` tool admits research use cases and structurally refuses clinical outputs.

Q: How is correctness enforced across languages?
A: Byte-level parity with the CPython reference runtime is enforced by test across three
implementations (CPython, Rust eager path, Rust indexed store); the shared certificate digest is
c0da17ffc80465258345c8a538171bfd868100cd883e9a20780a0dc5477e7ea4.

Q: What license?
A: Apache-2.0.
